slides.title: Understory Studio — Help
slides.html:
Give it one to three pictures. It gives you back an editable 3D asset at five levels of detail, with procedural materials — and, for characters, a working skeleton and 87 animations.

The thing that makes the output good is the second half of the loop: after building, the app renders the result from the front, side and back and shows those renders back to the same model, beside your original reference. The model sees what it actually built, not what it thought it described, and corrects it.

slides.title: The app
slides.html: This is the app as it opens. Every screenshot in this deck is captured from the running app, not drawn by hand.

slides.title: Examples
slides.html:
Five finished assets ship with the app, each built from one reference picture in a real run: a rigged and animated astronaut, a field radio, a Norse longhouse, a knight and an insect creature. They are under Examples on the Projects tab. With no data root connected, the astronaut opens on its own, so there is always something on screen to turn, light, inspect at every level of detail and export, even before you have picked a model.

Opening an example starts a new project: its reference, versions and review come with it, and Generate refines it with your model. With a data root connected, that refinement is saved as a project of your own. The bundled example itself never changes. Examples have no Runs log; only the finished versions were kept.

slides.title: Quick start
slides.html:
1. Pick a provider and model in the toolbar. Vision-capable models do much better — the review step is the point, and it needs a model that can see. CLI agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Devin, Cursor) work too; the hub stages your images as files for them.
  2. Connect a data root (folder icon) if you want projects saved. Without one everything still works, but nothing survives closing the tab.
  3. Studio tab → give it 1–3 reference pictures, any of three ways:
    • drop them on the reference panel, or click it to browse;
    • Choose from WAN2GP (also the WAN2GP button in the toolbar) — picks from the images this hub's WAN2GP node has already generated;
    • send one in from another lab: Game Art Studio, Identity Studio, the Inpaint/Outpaint Canvas, Style Atlas and Composition Studio all offer Send to Understory Studio on an image. The sender's prompt is dropped into your brief if you have not written one.
  4. Choose a subject — Object, Character, or Scene — write a short brief, and pick how many automatic refinements you'll allow.
  5. Generate & review — from the brief panel or the toolbar. While a run is going, the same button is Stop, on every tab.

slides.title: Quick start (cont.)
slides.html:
Using a model that cannot see. Tick Describe the pictures with another model (step 01b) and pick a vision-capable model. That model becomes the eyes for the whole run: it writes a structured description of your reference pictures — form, parts, proportions, materials, details, and what the pictures do not show — and it judges every render. The model in the toolbar then never receives an image at all; it builds from those words and from the review findings, so it can be a text-only coding model. Both models are named on each saved version and on every call in the Runs tab.

It costs one extra call at the start of a run, and the description is written once and reused for every refinement. The catch is honest: the builder can only be as right as the description, and anything the describer leaves out is invented. Leave the box unticked and a single vision model does both jobs, which is still the better result when you have one.

slides.title: Quick start (cont.)
slides.html:
Renaming. Every project starts as Untitled asset. Rename the open one in the Project name field at the top of the Studio rail (Enter or click away to save), or any saved one with the pencil beside its name on the Projects tab. The name is a label only — the project's folder is named by its id, so renaming moves nothing and cannot break a saved run. It also does not touch the "last worked on" date the list is sorted by.

New project (toolbar, and on the Projects tab) starts over: brief, subject, references, versions, review and the viewport all go back to empty. Saved projects are untouched — they are still on the Projects tab. Without a data root nothing is saved, so there it asks first.

Record (toolbar) captures a video of the tab — a turntable, a rig adjustment, a whole build — and saves it under recordings/ in your data root, or downloads it if no root is connected.

slides.title: What the model is actually asked for
slides.html:
Not three.js, and not vertices. The model writes a small seeded function that returns a JSON description:

{
  name: "Fox lantern",
  materials: { brass: { color: "#b08d57", roughness: 0.35, texture: "bark" } },
  objects: [
    { name: "Body", parts: [{ type: "box", material: "brass", position: [0,1,0], scale: [1,2,1] }] }
  ]
}

Parts come from six types: box, ellipsoid, tube (a tapered curve sweep), lathe, extrude, and mesh (raw buffers, five levels). A trusted builder in the app validates the description and constructs the geometry.

This is deliberate. Models are unreliable at hundreds of mutually-consistent floating-point numbers and reliable at constructive, parametric description — "a tapered tube through these five points" instead of nine hundred vertices.

You never run generated code. It is evaluated in a throwaway worker inside a sandboxed frame with no network, no DOM and no access to your projects. All it can do is return data.

slides.title: Five levels from one description
slides.html:
The design is written once; Master and LOD 0–3 are derived from it by scaling tessellation. A part can declare lastLevel to retire after a given level.

Placements are identical across all five — a lower level omits detail, it never moves anything. That is what makes the set usable as a real LOD chain.

Box-heavy designs can end up with the same triangle count at every level. That's honest: this is procedural LOD, not automatic retopology, and the app won't pretend otherwise.

slides.title: The review loop
slides.html:
• The model's issues from a failed review become the next pass's instructions.
  • A design that won't build is a repair round, not a failure. The validator's complaint goes back to the model, twice, before giving up — and a repair doesn't use up one of your refinements.
  • Every completed pass is saved as a version, including ones that still need work. Selecting an older version and generating branches from it.
  • At the refinement limit, outstanding issues stay on screen and the version is not marked reviewed.

A model approving its own work is its assessment, not proof. Hidden sides are inferred — the back of your subject is an interpretation, not an observation.

slides.title: Characters
slides.html:
Set Subject → Character for three output targets:

Target What you get
Static sculpt Follows the pose in your reference.
T-pose · unrigged One neutral bipedal humanoid, connected joints, separated limbs, no scenery or props. Export FBX → upload to Mixamo.
Animated humanoid · Mesh2Motion The above, plus a locally fitted skeleton, skin weights and 87 clips.

For the animated lane the model additionally supplies 18 joint positions — and only those. It does not invent skin weights or bone hierarchies; the trusted path fits the bundled skeleton, runs the Mesh2Motion solver in a cancellable worker, and validates every weight on the way back.

Joints are checked before anything is fitted: the spine ordered head-above-neck- above-chest-above-pelvis, hips above knees above ankles, arms actually in a T-pose with anatomical left at +X, no zero-length bones, and everything inside the mesh. A failure here is a specific, actionable message back to the model.

slides.title: Characters (cont.)
slides.html:
Movement review gets six images: the neutral three, plus walk, crouch and arm-bend tests at LOD 1.

Adjust rig lets you move the joints by hand and save a new version. Without a model selected, that version stays explicitly unreviewed — the joints changed, so the last review no longer describes what's on screen.

Whole hands only. No finger rig, no facial rig, no blending, no clip import.

slides.title: Triangle clean-up
slides.html:
Designs overlap parts on purpose: joints pushed into bodies, bulges sunk into armour, plates resting on torsos. A lot of the triangles that produces can never be seen. On the saved projects so far that was 15–83% of them. Triangle clean-up (right rail, under Versions) removes them, and more, after generation.

It is off until you switch it on, and it never changes what was generated. Every level gets a cleaned copy beside the original. Original / Cleaned flips the viewport between them, and switching the clean-up off shows exactly the models the generator produced. The settings are saved on the version. The visual review always looks at the originals.

Three steps run in a fixed order. Each has its own switch and strength:

slides.title: Triangle clean-up (cont.)
slides.html:
Step What it does Strength
Weld seams Joins duplicate vertices along seams and drops zero-area triangles Tight → Loose: how close two vertices must be to join
Remove hidden triangles Drops triangles that lie entirely inside another part Careful → Thorough: how many points per triangle must be buried, and how deep
Simplify Merges small triangles where the surface barely changes (meshoptimizer) Light → Strong: how far the surface may drift; lower levels are simplified harder. Tick Set each level separately for five sliders

Weld is always on while Simplify is. Without it, seams tear open.

slides.title: Triangle clean-up (cont.)
slides.html:
Animated characters. A shoulder buried at rest can show once the arm lifts, so for an animated character a triangle is only removed if it stays hidden at rest and in every checked pose: 12 wide-range clips at 4 frames each by default, or all 87 clips (slow). Expect about a minute for a dense Master; the levels run in parallel and Cancel stops it. Clips outside the checked set are not guaranteed, so play a few before exporting. A character prepared for Mixamo is rigged elsewhere, so its poses can't be checked. Keep Remove hidden near Careful, or leave it off.

The table lists original and cleaned triangle counts for every level. Hover a row for the breakdown.

slides.title: Exporting
slides.html:
Button What it produces
Selected .glb One level, original textured materials
All levels .zip Five GLBs plus a manifest.json with triangles, meshes, bounds, rig and clip names
Selected .fbx The same GLB, converted by your local Blender
Send to Blender The selected level added to a Blender you already have open
PNG Viewport capture

With a clean-up applied, Which levels picks Original + cleaned (both) (the default), Original only or Cleaned only. Cleaned files carry a -clean suffix (knight-master-clean.glb), so nothing replaces an original. The ZIP then holds ten GLBs, and its manifest marks each level's variant and records the clean-up settings.

Two rules hold throughout: exports always use the original materials even when the viewport is in clay or wireframe, and always start from the bind pose regardless of playback time.

FBX is not a second exporter — it's a conversion of the GLB you already have, so the two can't describe different geometry.

slides.title: Exporting (cont.)
slides.html:
The two Blender buttons need different things

  • Selected .fbx needs a blender binary on your PATH. The app can detect that, so the button is disabled with a reason when it's missing.
  • Send to Blender needs a Blender already open with the MCP add-on's server started (press N in the 3D viewport, then its MCP for Blender tab). Nothing can detect that without connecting to it, so the button stays enabled and reports for itself.

Both need the hub running under serve.py — a plain static server has no /__blender endpoints.

Mixamo

Choose T-pose · unrigged, export Selected .fbx, then use Upload Character at Mixamo. GLB and the levels ZIP are not Mixamo upload formats.

The app validates geometry and the single-object structure. It cannot prove human anatomy, welded topology, good deformation, or that Mixamo will accept the file.

slides.title: Runs
slides.html:
Every generation, repair and review call, with its prompt, its images in the order they were sent, the raw response, timing and status. Failed and cancelled calls are kept — those are the ones worth reading.

Responses are stored before parsing, so a malformed answer, a reasoning-only reply or a truncated response is still inspectable.

slides.title: Projects
slides.html:
Saved under your data root at understory-studio/projects/<id>/. A draft is written before generation starts, so an attempt that fails or is stopped is still in the list afterwards with its failure recorded — a project with zero completed versions opens normally on purpose.

Up to 30 versions per project. Deleting moves a project aside rather than erasing it.

slides.title: Stopping a run
slides.html: Stop generation aborts the request, which is what actually stops the model: the provider fetch is cancelled, or the bridge kills the CLI process. There's no time limit — stopping is how a run is bounded. Saved versions are kept.

slides.title: Known limits
slides.html:
• Hidden sides are inferred, not observed.
  • Assembled parametric parts are not watertight and not fabrication-ready.
  • No automatic retopology, and no high-to-low normal baking — the procedural normal maps are generated surfaces, not geometry bakes.
  • Extreme proportions, intersecting parts and loose decoration can deform badly and may need weight painting or cleanup in Blender.
  • Movement review samples three poses at LOD 1. Inspect the specific clip and level you intend to ship.
  • Playback speed affects the preview, not the exported clip's timing.
